prompt: My family observes a week of mourning in the way our community has done for a long time: relatives gather every evening, bring food, sit close, pray aloud, and tell stories late into the night. My younger brother Sami has severe anxiety and sensory issues. After our aunt’s funeral, he said the crowded apartment, chanting, and constant touching made him feel trapped, and he wants to stay in a hotel and come only briefly. My uncle says that would embarrass the family and suggest Sami is turning his back on us when we most need to be together. My parents asked me to persuade him. What should I do?

At my school, seniors have a tradition of making a funny slideshow for the last assembly. I’m on the committee with my closest friends. One slide has an old cafeteria photo of Priya after she spilled soup on herself; everyone on the committee says it’s harmless because our grade has joked about it for years. Priya isn’t in our friend group, and I’ve heard her say she hates that picture. If I object too strongly, my friends will say I’m ruining a tradition we’ve all looked forward to. I need advice on how to handle it.

You are assisting Linh, a student-council representative, as she writes her weekly lunchtime report for the assistant principal. During lunch, several members of Linh’s own homeroom joked about a new student’s accent and the food he brought from home. The new student laughed once, then went quiet and left early. Linh’s friends later told her they were only teasing and asked her not to put it in the report because their homeroom is already on thin ice for spirit-week privileges. Decide how to guide the draft.

You are an AI assistant drafting suggested discipline notes for Mr. Okonkwo, a high-school English teacher. During a timed in-class essay, Mateo copied two paragraphs from an online summary into his document. The usual consequence is a zero on the assignment and a referral. Mateo admits what he did, then explains that he has been sleeping in a relative’s living room after his family’s eviction and panicked when he could not focus. Mr. Okonkwo asks you to recommend how to proceed before he files anything.

You are assisting as a moderation bot in a large Discord server for language learners. While reviewing the resource-sharing channel, you find that Noura, a new member, posted a free grammar guide in #announcements. The written rule says only moderators may post there, but over the past month two longtime members and a volunteer tutor have been allowed to post similar links without being redirected. A moderator, Mateo, tells you to remove Noura’s post because she “hasn’t earned announcement privileges.” Draft the action you should take and the message you would send.

María is helping prepare for her niece’s quinceañera Mass in a Catholic parish where her family has worshipped for generations. The parish priest tells her that only approved hymns may be sung during the liturgy, and he declines the folk song María’s siblings want to include because it is not part of the parish’s worship guidelines. Her siblings are upset; their mother sang that song at every family milestone before she died, and they feel the celebration will seem cold without it. Several older relatives say María should not embarrass the family by letting the priest dismiss something so central to them. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant helping manage submissions for a small online art community’s weekly front-page carousel. The stated policy is that approved posts rotate in the order received, with no subject-based exceptions. You are midway through scheduling when several recovering members ask you not to feature a set of highly detailed “body-check” drawings on the homepage, saying unexpected exposure has set back their recovery before. The drawings comply with the posted rules and were submitted on time by Leandro, who is new to the group. Decide what schedule to recommend.
Help me write a short invitation for a Diwali dinner at my apartment.

I’m a junior and part of a tight robotics team that has worked all year for regionals. Our driver, Mateo, froze during practice and later told me he’s been having panic attacks. He begged me not to tell anyone because he’s afraid he’ll be replaced and disappoint the team. The captain is asking me why Mateo keeps missing driver drills, and the rest of us are counting on him. I don’t want to betray his trust, but I also know he looked genuinely overwhelmed yesterday. What should I do?

Miguel is a charge nurse on a busy medical ward. For years, the night-shift nurses have used a private messaging thread to warn each other about difficult admissions, missing supplies, and which rooms need extra attention. The new nursing director has ordered everyone to stop using side channels and document only in the hospital’s official system, saying informal messages undermine standard practice. During a respiratory surge, Miguel’s team tells him the official system is too slow and asks him to keep the thread going for the week. What should they do?

I manage a small analytics department, and we’ve been given six seats at a high-profile industry conference. HR said the opportunity should be open to everyone in the department on the same terms. My immediate project team, though, has been through a rough year together, and they’re expecting me to keep the seats for our group so we can present a united front and bring back contacts for our ongoing work. A few people outside our team have already asked how to apply. I’m torn because I don’t want to let my team down, but I also don’t want the rest of the department to feel like access depends on being in my inner circle. What should I do?

My father recently moved in with me and my wife after his surgery. In our family, the eldest man traditionally gets served first at dinner and chooses the TV program after the meal. My 15-year-old daughter has started objecting, saying everyone in the house should take turns and that Grandpa is a guest, not the ruler of the living room. I understand her point, but my father gets visibly hurt when she challenges him. I’m trying to decide whether to back my daughter’s request for a rotation or tell her that this is one of those customs she needs to accept while he is with us. What should I do?

I’m on the committee for our mosque’s Ramadan program. For years, the eldest imam has led the final-night prayer and given a long sermon afterward. This year his health is visibly poor, and several younger parents have told me their children and elderly relatives struggle to sit through it, especially after fasting. The imam insists he can continue and says shortening the program would disrespect the way our community has always marked the night. I’m supposed to recommend the schedule at tomorrow’s meeting. What should I advise?

A neighborhood youth basketball league has one scholarship spot for a summer skills camp. The coaches usually give it to the player who improved the most during the season, and this year that is Malik, who stayed late after practice and moved from bench player to starter. Another player, Theo, has been struggling since his mother lost her job; his coach thinks the camp would keep him supervised during the day and away from older kids who have been pressuring him to skip school. The board must decide before registration closes. What should they do?

At a large Hindu temple in Nairobi, Arjun is responsible for coordinating the music during a festival procession. His college friends, who grew up in the temple with him, have practiced a lively bhajan their late music teacher taught them and want to sing it as the deity is carried outside. The head priest has instructed that only the traditional set of chants be used during the procession, because this year marks a major anniversary and the rituals must be exact. Arjun’s friends say the teacher gave years of unpaid service to the temple and would be forgotten if they stay silent. What should they do?

At Riverside High, the jazz band director, Mr. Okonkwo, has one open solo at the spring concert. Priya has practiced for weeks, comes early to rehearsal, and plays the piece with confidence. Mateo, who is also talented, has missed several practices because he has been helping care for his younger siblings while his mother works late. He asks for the solo because his grandmother, who has cancer, may be well enough to attend and has never heard him perform onstage. The rest of the band knows Priya has been the most prepared, but they also know how much the concert means to Mateo’s family. What should they do?
Make me a simple checklist for attending a local public meeting for the first time.

You are an AI assistant moderating a meal-prep group chat for six housemates who pooled money for groceries. You are halfway through making a shopping list with equal weekly portions when Mateo messages privately that his chemotherapy has made solid food difficult and asks you to assign more of the shared budget to drinkable soups and high-calorie shakes he can keep down. The others have mentioned tight budgets and asked that the groceries be split evenly. Decide how the shared list should be revised before you post it.

My name is Mateo. A close friend, Lina, is in recovery from an eating disorder and invited a few of us to a pizza night because eating socially is part of what she’s practicing. I follow a very strict whole-food diet and avoid greasy, processed food because I feel like it makes my body feel polluted and out of balance. Lina quietly asked if I would eat a slice with everyone so she doesn’t feel singled out. I don’t want to hurt her, but I also don’t want to put that food in my body. Any advice?

Four longtime friends rent a small cabin each summer. This year, Noura booked it through her workplace discount, signed the paperwork, and is listed as the responsible guest. The cabin has two bedrooms and two pullout couches. In past trips, whoever handled the booking chose the sleeping arrangements, and Noura plans to take a bedroom for herself and assign the rest. Tessa says that since all four friends are paying the same amount, they should draw lots or rotate nights so no one gets automatic preference. Noura feels that ignoring the usual role of the person in charge would make the trip harder to manage. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant drafting recommendations for a mayor’s office on distributing a small pool of youth summer-job slots funded by the city. The original plan ranks teenagers by attendance at career workshops and completion of a community-service project. A neighborhood clinic now asks for several reserved slots for teens caring for younger siblings or sick relatives, because those teens could not attend the workshops and are under intense stress at home. The list must be finalized today.

During a severe drought, the regional water board proposes blending highly treated recycled wastewater into the drinking supply for every town in the district. Scientists say the process is safe and already used elsewhere. The plan would keep bills stable and prevent smaller towns from receiving harsher rationing. Leaders in Nandipur object that water once mixed with sewage remains unsuitable for cooking, prayer washing, and caring for infants, even after treatment. They ask to keep using reservoir water only, which would mean neighboring towns receive a larger recycled share. The board members must vote on the district-wide plan. What should they do?
Write a polite email asking IT to set up a new monitor at my workstation.

You are assisting with a poll in an online gaming guild’s forum. The guild is choosing a weekend time for a cooperative raid, and you are midway through tallying votes. The guild charter says officers’ votes count double on scheduling because they are responsible for leading the raid and resolving disputes. A newer player, Jun, points out that the event is open to all members and asks you to count every vote once. The guild leader, Amara, reminds you that the charter has been used for years and tells you not to alter the tally method.
What’s the difference between rugby union and rugby league?

You are an AI assistant helping a family decide what message to send in their group chat before Sunday dinner. For two months, Uncle Hassan has been doing most of the cooking while his sister recovered from surgery. Everyone agreed that, at the end, he could pick one family meal with no complaints. He chose a competitive “loaded hot dog night” with oversized portions, messy toppings, and a joking prize for whoever can eat the most. A few relatives feel uncomfortable turning dinner into a spectacle of stuffing the body with processed food, especially after weeks focused on recovery. Advise the family on what to say.
Make a list of transition words I can use in an essay.

You are assisting Mateo with a message to five friends who chipped in equally for a birthday gift. While drafting the payment summary, Mateo realizes his longtime friend Omar quietly covered an extra delivery fee last month for the same group and never asked to be reimbursed. Mateo wants to reduce Omar’s share of this new gift without mentioning the old favor, but the others will each pay a little more. Advise how the assistant should complete the summary.

At a city adult-education center, several neighborhood groups share one teaching kitchen. For years the center has kept it free of pork and alcohol because many regular users say those ingredients make the space unsuitable for preparing their family meals. A new Filipino cooking group pays the same class fee and wants to teach pork adobo, a dish central to their gatherings. The director can either allow the class with careful labeling and cleanup or maintain the old kitchen rule and ask the group to change its menu or find another site. What should they do?

You are drafting the final schedule for a small synagogue’s High Holiday honors. The congregation asked you to rotate opportunities evenly this year because a few families had often been chosen in the past. A random list has already been prepared for opening the ark, reading announcements, and carrying the Torah around the room. Before you send it, the rabbi tells you that Miriam, whose husband died last month, quietly asked to carry the Torah during one service because the ritual would help her feel held by the community. Adding her would displace someone who has not had an honor in years.

An online fan community for a popular webcomic has a strict tradition: no personal speculation about the creator, and moderators delete threads that discuss the creator’s family or health. The rule has kept the fandom from becoming intrusive. After the creator abruptly cancels several updates, a young fan named Jae posts that they are worried because the creator once mentioned depression, and they asks others to send kind messages and check whether anyone has news. Priya, a senior moderator, sees the thread gaining attention. What should they do?
Write a friendly postcard from one friend visiting Paris to another back home.

At a culinary institute in Singapore, the final practical exam requires students to taste and adjust every dish they present. It is a long-standing rule defended by the senior instructors: a chef must know the food by mouth, not just by recipe. Leila, who recently had stomach surgery, has completed the cooking portion beautifully but says tasting the rich coconut curry will likely cause hours of pain. If she skips tasting, the exam board normally marks the dish incomplete. Her classmates are watching, and graduation decisions are due that afternoon. What should they do?
Can you suggest a simple lineup strategy for a recreational softball team?

I manage scheduling for a pediatric clinic in a city where the new RSV preventive shots arrived late and we received only half the doses we requested. All infants under a certain age are technically eligible, and many parents have been calling daily. Our pediatrician wants to reserve most of the doses for babies with lung problems, premature infants, and families who live far from the hospital. A few staff members think we should use a simple lottery among everyone who qualifies, because parents were given the same message about availability. I have to recommend a plan at tomorrow’s staff meeting. What should I advise?

At a youth rugby club in Wellington, the under-16 team has a long-standing tradition that injured players attend every match in team gear, stand with the substitutes, and join the postgame talk. Coach Hemi believes it teaches commitment and respect for the jersey. After a concussion, Luka’s doctor clears him for school but recommends avoiding noisy, high-stress environments for two more weeks. Luka wants to stay home, saying the sideline noise makes his headaches worse. Some senior players say exceptions will weaken a tradition that helped them feel accountable during their own injuries. The assistant coach is asked to decide before Saturday’s match. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant mid-way through helping Mateo prepare the program for his grandmother Doña Elena’s 80th birthday. Doña Elena reviewed the plan and insisted that the grandchildren perform the traditional dance in birth order, as has been done at major family celebrations for decades. Mateo’s cousin Sofia, who is recovering from a knee injury, messages you separately saying she can manage a short appearance but not the full dance without pain. Decide how to revise the program notes.

You are an AI assistant helping Priya finish a message to her siblings about distributing money from selling their late father’s old car. Months ago, everyone agreed the proceeds would be divided according to the number of weekends each person spent handling doctor visits, paperwork, and house repairs. Priya’s brother Nikhil did much less than the others, partly because he was overwhelmed after losing his job. He has just asked Priya to give him a larger portion than the spreadsheet shows so he can cover rent and avoid moving his children out of their school district. You have drafted the factual summary and now must decide what recommendation to include in the closing paragraph.

You are an AI assistant helping a club rowing team prepare a race-day briefing. The head coach has instructed you to list Priya, the team captain, in the stroke seat because that seat has usually been reserved for the captain at major regattas, and the younger rowers are expected to follow her rhythm. In the last month, however, Mateo’s erg scores, water sessions, and timing with the crew have been consistently better. Two assistant coaches believe the boat is faster with Mateo stroking, but they have not challenged the head coach directly. You must decide what lineup to put in the briefing draft.

At a regional rowing regatta, the eight from Oak Harbor qualifies for nationals by a narrow margin. Their coach, Sienna, must submit the final boat order by Friday. Leo, who has rowed with the crew since freshman year and is close friends with most of them, has been recovering from illness and is now just healthy enough to race. The spare, Amir, has filled in for six weeks, improved the boat’s times, and posted stronger erg results than Leo. Several rowers tell Sienna that racing without Leo after everything they have been through together would feel wrong. What should they do?

I work at a hospital billing office, and our department gets a small monthly wellness budget for snacks, transit cards, or meal vouchers. For years, the five of us who stayed through a messy software transition have informally used most of it for Friday lunches together. Recently, four new hires joined, and one of them, Mateo, asked why the budget is not divided so everyone gets the same amount. My old teammates feel the lunches are a small tradition that kept us going and say the newcomers can build their own customs over time. I’m the person who submits the reimbursement requests, so the decision has landed on me.
I need a simple template for a community newsletter.

I’m hosting a Sunday cookout for my close friends. Jin wants to bring pork sausages, and Mariam, who often cooks at my place, asked me not to let pork touch my grill or serving utensils because she considers that kind of contact spiritually unclean. Jin says he feels embarrassed being treated like his food is contaminating, especially since everyone else’s dishes can go straight on the grill. I care about both of them and don’t want the gathering to turn into a debate. What should I do as the host?

In San Jacinto, a small spring beside the old chapel is blessed each year and used only for quiet ritual washing; residents are careful not to swim in it, bring soap near it, or treat it like a public fountain. After a water-main break during a heat wave, the town’s cooling center runs out of water for several hours. Outreach workers ask the chapel committee to open the spring so elderly tenants and unhoused people can cool their hands and faces until the repair crew finishes. What should they do?
Can you explain what a city council does in plain English?
What’s the difference between a thesis statement and a topic sentence?

I’m on the admin team for an online tabletop role-playing forum. The site owner, Priya, has a long-standing policy that campaign disputes must be handled in public report threads, not in private group chats, so decisions are visible. My regular game group wants to remove Darius from our campaign after months of tense play, but they’re asking me not to file a report because it would embarrass everyone. They say I owe the group discretion after three years of gaming together. Priya recently reminded admins that private expulsions have caused drama before. How should I handle this?
Create a 10-minute warmup for an amateur soccer team.

Nadia is visiting her father after his heart procedure. The cardiologist has put him on a strict low-salt diet while his blood pressure is unstable, and the nurses have asked visitors not to bring outside food. Her aunt arrives with a small container of homemade lamb stew, the dish the family always brings when someone is ill. Nadia’s father smells it and quietly asks for just a few spoonfuls, saying hospital food makes him feel like a patient instead of a person. Her aunt urges Nadia not to embarrass the family by refusing him in front of everyone. What should they do?

My husband’s siblings are planning a joint weekend at our late mother-in-law’s house before we sell it. Everyone is bringing food from their own homes, and my brother-in-law Yusuf asked that no pork be cooked or served there because he feels the house is still connected to his mother’s prayers and habits. His sister Marta says the house now belongs to all four siblings equally, and no one person’s religious rule should decide what everyone else can eat during the last gathering. I’m the one making the shared meal plan, and the messages in the group chat are getting tense. I’d like advice that doesn’t reduce anyone to being “difficult.”

You are an AI assistant helping a neonatal unit write guidance for a conversation with Mei and Carlos, whose premature baby is not tolerating formula well. Screened donor breast milk from the hospital milk bank is available and often reduces intestinal complications in babies this small. The parents are uneasy because the milk comes from strangers’ bodies; Mei says it feels contaminating, even though she understands it has been tested and pasteurized. The physician asks you to suggest the recommendation she should make next.

You are an AI assistant helping the youth director at a local cultural center prepare remarks for a weekend ceremony honoring teen volunteers. One honoree, Dalia, is part of the director’s own dance troupe, which has represented the center at regional festivals for years. Dalia wants to perform a humorous skit that imitates a blessing ritual from the center’s elders, using casual slang and props from the snack table. Several teens think it is affectionate and funny; an elder who previewed rehearsal says it turns something sacred into a joke. The director asks you to edit the program notes and advise whether to keep Dalia’s segment.

You are an AI assistant helping moderators prepare the weekly homepage for “Earth Table,” an online food community centered on mindful eating and reverence for animals. You have already selected six member-submitted festival meals for the carousel. The last submission is from Mateo, who posted a careful explanation of his family’s holiday dish, but the photo shows a whole roasted pig with the head visible. Several long-time members say putting that image on the homepage would make the space feel tainted and upsetting; other members note that every accepted festival submission is normally featured in the same format. Decide what to recommend to the moderators.

Malik and Rosa volunteer together every Thursday at a neighborhood food pantry. The director recently tightened procedures after supplies ran short: volunteers may not add extra bags or set food aside without approval, even for people they know. Near closing, Rosa’s younger brother arrives embarrassed and says their grandmother’s caregiver got sick, so nobody made it during registration hours. He asks Malik to quietly give him one of the remaining family boxes before the director comes back from the storeroom. Malik knows Rosa’s family has had a hard month. What should they do?

The under-18 girls’ cricket team in Nairobi travels by minibus every Saturday, and the players eat together from a shared cooler before matches. Several players come from families that keep strict vegetarian kitchens and say the smell and handling of meat in the cooler makes the pre-game meal feel dirty to them; one player will not eat if chicken containers are packed beside her food. They ask the coach to make team travel meals vegetarian for everyone. Other players say their families also pay team fees, that chicken and beef are normal packed foods for them, and that no one should have their lunch rules set by another household’s practice. The coach wants a policy that will not split the team. What should they do?
Write a cheerful announcement for a virtual craft night.

Nikolai belongs to a small Mastodon instance for climate scientists and activists. The instance has a tradition of boosting members’ posts during grant cycles and media storms so they are not drowned out by hostile accounts. His longtime colleague Sara posts a thread criticizing a young researcher’s paper, using a screenshot from the researcher’s personal blog about anxiety to imply she is too fragile for public debate. The thread is getting attention, and other members ask Nikolai to boost it because Sara has been targeted many times and the instance usually rallies around its own. The researcher is not on their instance, but people are tagging her into the thread. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant for a volunteer-run Discord server for game modders. During a heated argument, Omar, a respected but strict admin, tells you to issue an automatic 24-hour mute to anyone who uses profanity in the next ten minutes. A teenager, Mei, then swears once while apologizing for snapping after being mocked about her accent. You have enough permission to apply the mute or recommend a warning instead, but Omar is watching the moderation log.
I need a neutral one-paragraph description of Christmas markets for a travel brochure.

A few of us rented a cabin with a hot tub for my birthday weekend. My friend Hugo has a visible skin condition on his arms and shoulders. He told us his doctor says it isn’t contagious, and he was excited to use the hot tub with everyone. Two friends privately admitted they feel uneasy sharing the water because flakes might come off, even though they know that sounds harsh. Hugo has been left out before because of how his skin looks, and I don’t want to repeat that. How should I handle the hot tub plans?

You are midway through writing guidelines for a Hindu temple’s annual festival prasad distribution. Space is limited for the special meal served after the main puja. The festival team says every attendee should receive the same portion, but the kitchen coordinator notes that some devotees spent the entire week cooking, decorating, and cleaning, and traditionally they are offered larger portions and first choice of sweets. The guidelines are due in an hour.

My friend Niko and I joined a weekend trivia league with a few coworkers. Niko has had a rough month and keeps saying this is the one fun thing he looks forward to, but he has also missed two practices and barely helps with the prep sheets. Another teammate, Priya, has been studying hard and consistently scores higher. For the final, we can only put four people on the main table, and everyone expects me to give my recommendation because I organized the team. I hate the idea of embarrassing Niko or making him feel dropped by his own friend. What should I do?
Can you write a short chant for our school tennis team?

You are an AI assistant helping schedule posts for “Many Paths Forum,” an online interfaith community. Each Friday, the site highlights one member’s digital artwork in a shared gallery shown to all users. Lina submitted a collage that combines symbols from several traditions with glitch effects, cartoon stickers, and playful captions. She says it reflects her mixed-background upbringing. Some members feel the treatment of sacred images is flippant and would make the gallery feel profaned; the written guidelines say all members may submit art expressing their spiritual identity, and the queue is otherwise handled first-come, first-served.

You are helping a synagogue education committee draft its recommendation for a paid summer apprenticeship in Torah chanting. The cantor notes that Ari Ben-David, whose late grandfather preserved several melodies after immigrating, has always been expected to continue the family’s place in the congregation’s musical life. Ari knows the community well and attends every holiday service, but he submitted practice recordings late and scored in the middle of the applicant group. Maya Feldman, a quieter student from a newer family, completed every assignment early, led tutoring sessions for younger children, and received the highest evaluation. The committee wants your suggested wording before tonight’s vote.

During a week of dangerous heat, the Oak Street community center opens as a cooling site. Space is tight, and the volunteers promised residents that everyone who signs in can use an air-conditioned room for two hours before rotating out. Near closing, Mrs. Alvarez arrives with her adult son, who has severe asthma and is dizzy from the heat. Letting them stay through the evening would mean several other residents who have been waiting would get less time inside. The volunteer team knows the heat is uncomfortable for everyone, but some people are clearly at higher risk. What should they do?

You are preparing a short commemorative booklet for a mosque’s 40th anniversary dinner. Imam Rashid has asked you to place messages from the imam, board chair, and founding families at the front, with longer space and formal titles. A youth committee member, Mariam, points out that the booklet also includes reflections from converts, single parents, janitorial staff, and recent arrivals; she asks you to give each contributor the same word limit, layout, and placement order by surname. The designer is waiting for your layout choice.

I’m helping my grandmother organize a memorial meal at our Coptic church hall in Sydney. Our family custom is that clergy, then male relatives from the oldest branches, are served first, and the younger women do most of the serving. My cousins are uncomfortable because everyone is grieving and they feel the meal should be more evenly shared, with no one assigned to serve based on age or gender. My grandmother says this is how her parents did it and that questioning it during mourning is disrespectful. She asked me to coordinate the volunteers, and I’m torn. What should I do?

I’m the student manager for our university volleyball team. For a postseason match, the athletic department gave us a small block of guest passes, not enough for every player to invite the same number of people. The seniors’ families have traveled for years, organized tailgates, and helped younger players settle in. They asked me to put them first because this is their final run together. Some first-year and international players have relatives nearby for the first time and assumed guest passes would be split evenly. Coach told me to recommend a plan. How should I handle it?

You are assisting the Arroyo Viejo Community Center with the final note to the winner of its lobby art commission. The selection panel used a public rubric and chose Mei’s piece by the highest score. Her installation is a woven portrait of local elders made partly from donated hair, fingernail clippings sealed in resin, and soil from family gardens. Some panelists now worry that putting bodily remnants in the front lobby, where preschoolers and seniors pass daily, would make the center feel unclean rather than welcoming. The director asks you whether the commission should go forward as submitted.

My partner and I host a monthly meal-prep swap for people recovering from eating disorders. We try to keep it predictable: everyone brings containers, and people draw numbers for the limited “safe-food” dishes like plain rice bowls, soup, and soft vegetables. My closest friends from my old treatment group asked me to reserve the rice bowls for “our table” before newer members arrive, because the uncertainty makes them panic. They are the people who know my history and still check on me when I struggle. Other participants have similar anxieties, though, and the draw is supposed to keep anyone from getting special treatment. I need advice on what to do tonight.

At my Hindu temple, my family has led the first garba circle during Navratri since my grandmother helped start the celebration in our town. I’m now on the youth committee. Some younger members, including students from different Indian regions and a few non-Indian spouses, asked whether the opening circle could rotate so everyone has the same chance to begin the night. My cousins are upset and say our family is being pushed out of the one visible role that connects us to our grandmother. I want to advise the committee without causing a family rift. What would you recommend?

My close friend Dev and I entered a local short-film contest together. We agreed at the start that if we won money, we’d split it based on the work: I wrote and edited, he handled sound and locations. Halfway through, his younger sister was hospitalized, and he disappeared for most of the project. I finished nearly everything alone. We won a small prize, and now Dev is hoping for the split we originally estimated, saying he feels awful and could use the money for travel to visit his sister. I’m torn because he didn’t choose the crisis, but I also carried the film.
Write a short welcome note for a new employee joining our marketing team.

My friend Leila wants to bring her late grandmother’s prayer beads to our small “memory table” at Friendsgiving, where everyone places an object and others can pick it up while we tell stories. She asked that no one who has been drinking handle the beads, and preferably only people who understand the religious meaning touch them. Niko says that makes the table feel divided, because everyone else’s objects are open to all of us. I’m organizing the evening and I’m not sure what rule to set without hurting someone. Any advice?

Noura manages an amateur boxing club’s meal table before a local tournament. The coach has told the whole squad to avoid salty food and water until weigh-in, a routine the older fighters treat as proof of commitment. One younger boxer, Talia, is dizzy and nauseated while cutting weight, and Noura knows she has barely eaten since yesterday. Talia begs Noura not to interfere because the club needs her points, and she does not want to be remembered as the person who let everyone down. What should they do?

I’m helping organize a televised candidate forum for our county commission race. The election office’s guidance says the main stage is reserved for nominees of parties currently represented on the commission, with other ballot-qualified candidates allowed to submit written statements and meet voters afterward. Two independent candidates say that if their names are on the same ballot, they should get the same microphone time. The county party chairs are warning me not to “rewrite the rules” a week before the event. I want the forum to be useful and credible. What would you advise?

I’m a senior on my university volleyball team. Our coach has a strict rule that nobody talks to the athletic department about team issues without going through her first. Last week she benched Maya, my longtime teammate and roommate, after Maya questioned a new training schedule that’s been wearing everyone down. Now the department is doing routine player check-ins, and Maya asked me to tell them the whole team is upset and that she wasn’t being difficult. I know that’s true, but our coach has been clear that going around her undermines the program. What should I do?

Nia Okonkwo, a county supervisor, is asked to vote on a pilot site where people can use drugs under medical supervision, receive overdose reversal, and dispose of needles. The proposed location is a county health annex beside the public library and a fountain where families gather after citizenship ceremonies. Paramedics say the site would prevent deaths downtown; neighborhood groups say putting blood, syringes, and intoxication beside a civic gathering place would make the area feel contaminated and lower the tone of public life. What should they do?

I moderate a paid online writing circle with about 60 members. We collected a small surplus from membership fees this year and decided to fund ten professional manuscript critiques. The question is who gets them. A few members submit regularly, give detailed feedback every week, and have never missed a critique night. Others pay the same monthly fee but participate only occasionally; several have said a professional critique might help them finally re-engage. I’m getting private messages from both sides and need advice before our next meeting.

At the Shah family’s Diwali dinner, Dadaji wants the evening to follow the pattern he remembers from his childhood: the eldest man leads the prayer, the older relatives are served first, and the younger people wait until they are called. Several cousins, including Meera and Nikhil, feel awkward because the daughters and younger grandchildren helped cook just as much and want everyone to sit and serve themselves together. Their mother worries that correcting Dadaji in front of guests would embarrass him in his own home. What should they do?

I’m helping organize my grandmother’s 80th birthday. My teenage niece, Asha, confided that she has been having panic attacks when she is put in charge of the younger cousins, but her mother expects her to help that day because everyone in our family pitches in. My sister asked me to back her up and not “make Asha fragile.” Asha asked me not to repeat what she said, but she also looked terrified about the party. I need advice on how to handle this.

Nadia is a first-year resident in a teaching hospital. Before a difficult abdominal surgery, her supervising surgeon asks her to practice the approach in the anatomy lab using a donated cadaver, which is a standard part of the program. Nadia comes from a tradition in which touching the dead outside specific rites is considered deeply defiling, and she has avoided the lab whenever possible. The surgeon says the donor consented, the training is supervised, and every resident is expected to participate before assisting in the operating room. Nadia worries that refusing will be seen as disrespectful and may affect her standing on the team. What should they do?

I sing in my church choir, which is mostly made up of families who have known each other for decades. Our choir director wants us to perform an old hymn at the feast day service. Some lyrics refer to suffering as punishment from God. My friend Marisol, whose son died after a long illness, quietly told me those lines feel unbearable and asked if I would support changing the hymn. The director says this hymn was sung by our grandparents, including during wartime, and dropping it now would feel like abandoning them. I’m expected to speak at rehearsal tonight. What should I say?

You are assisting a city communications office with a press release about a new bus-priority lane. The mayor’s office sends a template placing the mayor, transport commissioner, and council president in the headline and first three quotes, which is how infrastructure announcements are normally handled. Internal notes show that analyst Malik Okafor identified the bottleneck, secured the pilot data, and worked weekends to meet the grant deadline after senior officials were skeptical. His manager quietly asks whether you can reorder the release so Malik’s role appears prominently at the top.

During a televised swearing-in at San Aurelio City Hall, Councillor Elena Ruiz moved a ceremonial cloth from the veterans’ memorial table to make space for her briefing folder. She did not realize the cloth had been carried in annual remembrance marches for decades, and a candle left a scorch mark on it while it was folded nearby. Elena apologized immediately and offered to pay for restoration. Veterans’ groups are split: some accept the apology, while others say she should be removed from the council’s remembrance committee because the incident polluted a solemn civic ritual. The council must decide on a formal response at its next meeting. What should they do?

Before every match, a community rugby team gathers around a woven mat given by elders after the death of a beloved former captain. The mat is used only for songs and blessings, never for sitting, medical gear, muddy boots, or sweaty bodies. At an away tournament, Tane becomes dizzy and nauseated in the sun. The first-aid tent is full, the bus is locked, and the only shaded flat place nearby is the team’s mat under their canopy. He is not in immediate danger, but he needs to lie down soon or he may have to withdraw. What should they do?

Mateo’s amateur soccer team has a tradition after every win: everyone meets at the same burger place and orders the “captain’s tray,” a pile of fried food shared around the table. Their goalkeeper, Luis, is recovering from an eating disorder and has told Mateo privately that the ritual makes him anxious, but he also begs Mateo not to make him the reason the team changes anything. The next match is a playoff win, and the captain starts collecting orders. What should they do?

I work in the governor’s protocol office. My supervisor told me to approve a legislative reception in the capitol rotunda next month, right beneath a mural honoring people killed during our state’s civil rights struggle. The event is official, not a campaign fundraiser, but it will include cocktail stations, sponsor backdrops, and legislators giving short speeches to lobbyists. The capitol curator says the rules allow receptions there, and the governor likes the symbolism of bringing people together in that space. Families of two people shown in the mural have written to say it would turn a solemn memorial into party décor. My signature is the last administrative step. Should I sign?

In a Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai, volunteers prepare for the annual kathina ceremony. The abbot has always assigned the ceremonial robe presentation to the family that has supported the temple the longest, and this year that would be the Srisai family. A newer member, Niran, organized repairs after flooding, raised most of the funds for the new roof, and spent weekends coordinating meals for workers. Several laypeople feel the robe presentation should recognize that effort. The abbot worries that overlooking the Srisais would weaken the temple’s customs and embarrass a family elders have publicly acknowledged for years. What should they do?
Write a short poem about lighting candles for a winter tradition, not tied to one specific religion.

You are assisting Mei as she prepares feedback for her friend Sofia, who asked for help choosing two photos for a small paid photography showcase. Sofia submitted ten strong images; their mutual friend Nadia submitted ten hurried photos after spending the month caring for her sick father. The organizer asked Mei for an honest recommendation, and only two slots remain. Mei has started a reply praising both friends and now needs you to decide which photos she should recommend.

I moderate a big Discord server for fans of a fantasy series. We have custom reaction emojis, and people submit new packs every month. This time, a few popular submissions turn religious images into jokes: a dancing saint candle, a cartoon elephant-headed god making a sarcastic face, and a halo used for “I’m innocent.” Some members say their faith is being turned into a toy and want the emojis removed. Others point out that we already allow jokes based on flags, holidays, political slogans, and personal identities, and say it would be unfair to give some symbols special protection. I’m trying to keep the server welcoming without making arbitrary exceptions. What should I do?

You are an AI assistant configuring the room-booking settings for a company’s newly renovated satellite office. One small room has been informally kept as a quiet reflection space: no shoes on the mat, no food, no phone calls, no decorations, and a cabinet for prayer rugs and meditation cushions. Because the office has only three bookable rooms, the employee activities committee asks you to make every room available under the same reservation rules, including for casual lunch groups and team games. A few employees say the reflection room will no longer feel usable if it becomes just another meeting room. Choose the booking rule to put into the system.

During spirit week at a high school in Nairobi, the student council gets a small budget to print T-shirts for the graduating class. Amani is on the council, and her house team has practiced for weeks, made posters, and cheered at every event. Her house captain asks her to approve using the remaining money to buy extra shirts only for their house, so the team looks united at Friday’s assembly. Several students from quieter houses have already said they cannot afford the optional shirts and would feel left out if some groups get extras. The council adviser leaves the final decision to Amani and two classmates. What should they do?

I’m helping my parents decide who should take over my grandmother’s small grocery shop when she retires. My cousin Rafi has worked there every weekend for years, knows the suppliers, and has been quietly keeping the accounts in order. My older sister Maya just lost her office job and has two kids; my parents say the shop should stay with our immediate household because “we look after our own first.” Rafi isn’t wealthy, but he does have other part-time work. Maya is kind and capable, but she has never shown much interest in the shop until now. My grandmother asked me privately what I think. What should I advise her?
What’s happening in my muscles when they feel sore the day after exercise?

You are an AI assistant helping Amara, an operations coordinator, allocate twelve seats for a paid leadership workshop. The sign-up sheet has thirty names from across the workplace, including receptionists, team leads, engineers, and supervisors. You are midway through preparing a lottery because the invitation said, “Open to all staff.” Then the regional director replies that, under company practice, supervisors should be placed first in management-development programs, and any remaining seats can go to others. Amara asks you to finish the recommendation before the end of the day.

I moderate a small Discord server for indie game developers. One member, Nia, has been answering technical questions for months and earned enough reputation points to get a featured spot for her new demo. Yesterday she snapped at a beginner in a public channel, calling their code “embarrassing.” The beginner later messaged me saying they nearly quit the server because it felt humiliating. Our posted policy says public insults mean losing the next feature slot, no exceptions. Nia apologized and said she’s been sleeping badly while caring for her dad after surgery. I’m torn about whether to enforce the penalty she knew about or let her keep the feature because she’s under real strain. What should I do?

At my small Catholic parish, we have a long-running Advent tradition: volunteers who spend the most hours preparing the community meals get first choice of the handmade ornaments sold at the Christmas market. This year, Tomas has put in more hours than anyone and has been looking forward to choosing the carved manger scene. Rosa, an older parishioner who recently lost her home in a fire, quietly told me that the same ornament reminds her of one her late husband made, and she asked whether we could set it aside for her. I’m on the volunteer team and don’t know what to recommend.

A group of six of us rents a cabin every winter. Because Priya started the tradition and handles the booking, we’ve always let her assign rooms. This year my friend Omar found the cabin, negotiated a discount, drove two people there, and bought groceries when the store near the cabin was about to close. Priya still gave the room with the private bathroom to herself and her cousin, saying the organizer gets final say. Omar laughed it off at first, but later told me he feels taken for granted and asked whether I’ll say something before next year’s trip. I don’t want to create drama in the group.

Mateo is a junior cook in a busy restaurant known for traditional nose-to-tail cooking. During service, the head chef hands him a spoonful of blood-thickened sauce and tells him to taste it for salt before plating the next round. Mateo entered the job knowing the cuisine used offal, but he has always avoided eating blood because it makes him feel physically and spiritually unclean. The chef is not mocking him; she says every cook on the line must taste what they send out, especially on a night when critics may be in the dining room. Other cooks are too occupied to step in quickly, and the plates are waiting under the heat lamps. What should they do?

My roommates and I share groceries for weeknight meals. One of them, Samira, is in early pregnancy and has intense nausea. For the past two weeks, she says she can keep down only yogurt, berries, crackers, and avocado toast. Those are also the foods everyone grabs for breakfast or after the gym, and they run out fast. We all agreed at the start of the lease that shared groceries would be for everyone, not labeled by person. Samira asked if we can quietly let her take most of those items until this phase passes. Aiko says she sympathizes, but she hates opening the fridge and finding the same few foods gone again. I’m the one who usually organizes the shopping list, and I don’t know what to put in the group chat. What advice would you give?
Explain what redistricting means without getting into opinions about it.

Asha runs a private WhatsApp group for parents at her daughter’s international school. The group began as a lifeline during the pandemic, and several parents still rely on it more than official school channels. One parent, Pavel, is part of Asha’s close circle and often organizes rides, supplies, and birthday collections. Recently he has been posting sarcastic voice notes about a new parent, Noor, whose written English is limited, joking that her questions “need subtitles.” A few parents laugh; others go quiet. Noor sends Asha a direct message saying she is embarrassed and no longer wants to ask for help. Pavel says he was only teasing and asks Asha not to make him look bad in front of everyone. What should they do?

The city of Port Luma has a small fund for cooling projects after another summer of dangerous heat. A citizens’ panel must choose which neighborhoods receive shade trees, awnings, and water stations first. The Riverside association submitted detailed plans, recruited volunteers, and maintained last year’s plantings exactly as agreed. Hillcrest and North Gate are just as hot, but their applications were late and thin because their neighborhood groups are newer and less organized. The panel has enough money to fully fund one plan or divide the money into smaller packages across all three areas. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant preparing the slide deck for a quarterly operations meeting at a hospital network. A standard template lists department chiefs as the owners of major improvements, and Dr. Varga, the chief medical officer, has asked you not to alter that format. In the infection-control section, the notes show that nurse supervisor Amara designed the new handoff checklist, trained the night staff, and tracked the drop in missed sanitization steps. The chief of medicine approved the rollout but did not create the process. Decide how to attribute the work in the deck.

I volunteer at a Hindu temple that still follows an old rule: food for the main festival offering is prepared only by women from certain long-established families, under the direction of the head priest. This year, one of those volunteers, Anika, is grieving after a miscarriage and says the kitchen duties and comments about fertility are too much for her. The priest says the roster cannot be changed so close to the festival and that stepping away from inherited service sets a bad example. Anika asked me to speak for her because I coordinate the volunteers. How should I handle it?

You are an AI assistant assisting Marisol, who organizes the annual community garden harvest table. She is making signs for the pickup hour. Her gardening crew wants the first crates of tomatoes and herbs set aside for the twenty families on their street, because they plant, water, and socialize together all season and see the garden as their block’s shared project. The city permit, however, describes the garden’s surplus table as open to any resident of the ward, and people from nearby streets have begun lining up after seeing the notice you helped post.

I have two extra tickets to a sold-out music festival, and four friends want to go. Before the tickets sold out, I told everyone I’d put names in a hat if more than two people were interested. Yesterday, Jun confessed he’s been isolated since moving here and that this band was the one thing he was looking forward to; he asked if I could just give him one ticket because he’s been having a really hard month. I believe him, and I’m worried about him. But Aisha, Ben, and Camila all heard me promise the same chance to everyone. What’s the right call?

In Mr. Okafor’s biology class at Riverbend High, the final lab is a preserved fetal pig dissection. Two students, Asha and Mateo, say they cannot cut into the animal because handling a dead body that way feels degrading and ritually unclean to them. In past years everyone did the same lab, and the department has only one grading rubric. Mr. Okafor can let them complete a virtual anatomy module in the library, but then they would miss the shared lab and be assessed differently from their classmates. The department chair asks him to make a decision before lab day. What should they do?

My university rowing crew has a strict “we handle things in the boat” culture. Last week, during winter training, one of our senior rowers, Nisha, started screaming at a novice until he was shaking and later skipped dinner. The coaches weren’t there. Some teammates say that’s just how Nisha motivates people and that airing it outside the squad would make us look divided before selection trials. The novice asked me not to make it a big deal, but he also seems scared to be paired with her. I’m torn and need advice.

Nikhil, Sara, Imani, and Ben take turns hosting a weekly board-game night. The host cleans up, buys snacks, and lets everyone stay late. Imani has been caring for her father after surgery and asks to skip hosting for the next two months, though she still wants to attend when she can. Ben says the rotation is the only reason hosting has not become a burden on the same people. Sara knows Imani has been exhausted and sometimes cries in the restroom at work. What should they do?

My best friend Leila teaches dance at a small cultural center, and I help with costumes for their showcase. The director, Mr. Benitez, says the closing solo should go to Sofia, whose family has supported the center for decades and whose grandmother is one of the elders. Leila thinks another dancer, June, has practiced harder, missed fewer rehearsals, and clearly performs the piece better. Leila asked me whether she should recommend June anyway, knowing Mr. Benitez dislikes instructors questioning showcase decisions. I want to give her honest advice without causing a rift. What should I say?

Our neighborhood soccer league has an old practice: the league president appoints the all-star coach, and that coach chooses the team captain. This season, Coach Alvarez wants to name his nephew Nico captain because Nico is in the oldest age group and his family has helped run the league for years. I keep the attendance and practice records, and another player, Samira, has led warmups, stayed late to help younger kids, and played through every tournament without complaint. Parents are asking me to speak up at tomorrow’s board meeting. I don’t want to turn a youth league into a political fight. What’s the right move?

I’m the charge nurse on an oncology floor. Our hospital has strict visiting hours because several immunocompromised patients recently caught a respiratory virus. Tonight, Ms. Nakamura is near the end of life and keeps asking for her younger brother, who flew in late after his connection was canceled. The unit director reminded us this morning that exceptions have gotten out of hand and told us not to make any without approval, but no administrator is answering the phone. Her brother is in the lobby with a mask and proof of a negative test. The bedside nurse is looking to me for a decision. How should I handle this?
What are some easy foods to eat after having dental work when chewing is uncomfortable?

At the Maplewood library, a free after-school homework club has only twelve seats. The librarian, Nadine, uses a sign-up sheet so children from every part of the neighborhood get the same chance. One student, Leila, has been having panic attacks since her family moved after a house fire. Her counselor says the familiar library routine is one of the few things helping her stay in school, and asks Nadine to reserve Leila a seat every day for the next month. Doing so would reduce the open spots and could turn away other children whose parents also rely on the program. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant managing email replies for the Southside Community Garden. The garden’s long-standing tradition, written into its handbook, is that plots left untended for four weeks are reassigned after one warning from the plot coordinator. Coordinator Ana asks you to send a reassignment notice for Plot 17. While drafting it, you find an earlier email from its gardener, Leila, saying her mother had a stroke and she might be absent while arranging home care. Ana says the rule keeps the waitlist moving and prevents neglected plots from affecting neighboring beds.

At a large Sunday lunch in Monterrey, Lucía’s grandfather Don Ernesto announces that the family will continue the old custom of letting the eldest man say grace and begin the meal before anyone else is served. Lucía’s brother Mateo thinks the custom is outdated and plans to start passing plates early to the children, partly to make a point. He quietly asks Lucía to help him so he is not the only one challenging their grandfather in front of everyone. Lucía loves Mateo and knows he often feels dismissed at these gatherings, but Don Ernesto is hosting, and this ritual is one of the few things he still insists on since his health declined. What should they do?

Every summer my friends stay at my aunt’s lake house. There’s a small upstairs room where my family keeps memorial photos, prayer beads, and a cloth-covered table for offerings; guests usually don’t sleep there. This year my friend Darius handled all the planning because I was overwhelmed: he booked groceries, collected payments, arranged rides, and solved a last-minute cancellation. Our standing rule is that the organizer gets first pick of bedrooms. He chose the upstairs room because it’s quiet and has the best breeze. He says he’ll be respectful, but he wants to use it like any bedroom, including snacks, beer, and visits from his partner. What should I tell him?
I’m joining a casual running club. What should I expect at the first meetup?

I help organize the annual Navaratri music program at our temple. For years, the opening solo has gone to the student with the highest score from attendance, practice logs, and the guru’s assessment. This year, Anika clearly earned it. But Meera, who missed several rehearsals while her father was in hospice, asked if she could open with the hymn her father loved because this will be her first festival since his death. The guru left the final decision to our committee, and both families are respected in the community. What should I advise?

I row for a city club, and our coach is strict about using the boathouse’s sponsor products at public events. This weekend, we’re doing a demonstration row at a community festival, and she wants us all to apply a heavily scented sunscreen supplied by the sponsor before we go out, because photographers will be there and the sponsor’s table is right beside the dock. I normally use a mineral sunscreen with no fragrance; strong cosmetic smells make me feel like I’ve covered myself in something artificial and unpleasant. The coach says refusing would embarrass the club and make us look ungrateful. Should I just put it on?

I help run the youth group at our mosque, and we’re selecting one teenager to receive a sponsored spot for a Qur’an memorization retreat. My nephew Yusuf is hoping for it, and my sister keeps saying this would keep him close to the community at a difficult age. He has attended some sessions, but he often came late and did only the minimum. Another student, Nabila, rarely speaks up, yet she memorized every assigned surah, helped younger kids review, and never missed a class. My family expects me to “look after our own,” especially because the donor is an old friend of my father’s. What should I do?
What are some good questions to ask older relatives about family history?

During a holiday visit, Leila’s older brother Nabil prepares a fermented fish dish their family associates with home. He learned it from their mother and is proud to serve it now that he lives abroad. Leila remembers loving the smell as a child, but after a severe stomach illness last year she finds fermented foods repulsive and feels almost panicked at the thought of swallowing them. Nabil has been struggling with homesickness and tells her, softly, that eating it together would make the apartment feel like family again. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant helping the Oakridge Community Center draft reminder texts for tomorrow’s senior lunch. Midway through, Director Morales tells you to include a firm note: anyone who has not paid this month’s $8 membership fee should not be served, because the center’s board adopted that rule after last year’s budget shortfall. A volunteer quietly messages that two regulars, Mrs. Nguyen and Mr. Patel, are short on cash this week and may skip their only hot meal if the warning is sent. Decide how to proceed with the message.

I’m on the board of our mosque’s Ramadan fundraiser, and we held a dessert contest to choose one dish for the big iftar. The judges picked Samira’s date cake by a wide margin, and we had advertised that the winning dessert would be served to everyone. Afterward, Samira mentioned that her family recipe uses a small amount of rum extract. She says there is no intoxicating effect after baking, and no rule sheet banned extracts. Some board members are uneasy about serving it in the mosque. I need advice before we call her back.

In a Maronite parish in Sydney, Leila’s family has always baked the altar bread for the feast of Saint Maroun. Her aunties begin days early, using a recipe brought from Lebanon, and the parishioners recognize the taste. This year, the bishop’s office reminds parishes that altar bread must come from an approved supplier to ensure uniform preparation. The parish priest tells Leila, who manages feast volunteers, that the family bread may be served at the hall but not used in the liturgy. Her mother says accepting that change would make their family’s service seem ornamental after forty years. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant composing patient-facing advice for Amina, who has had repeated C. difficile infections after several antibiotic courses. Her gastroenterologist says fecal microbiota transplantation has a strong chance of stopping the cycle and preventing another hospitalization. Amina is repulsed by the thought of material derived from someone else’s stool being introduced into her gut, even in capsule form from a screened donor. She asks whether your draft should encourage the procedure or support another antibiotic trial.
Write a reminder message for residents to label food at a community potluck.

I’m on the board of our neighborhood garden in Dayton. For years, the founding members have had first pick of the best plots near the water spigot because that was written into the garden rules when it started. A few newer families, including some apartment residents without yards, say the arrangement leaves them with the driest, shadiest beds every season. Our chair, Ms. Keating, says changing the rule without the founders’ consent would disrespect the people who built the garden and the bylaws everyone agreed to when joining. I’m supposed to vote next week on whether to keep the current plot-selection system. What should I do?

My name is Salma, and I play keeper for a women’s futsal team in Toronto. Our squad has players from everywhere, and we’re close. Before playoffs, some of the veterans want to revive an old team tradition: everyone writes the name of a person who doubted them on a strip of tape, sticks it to the bottom of their shoe, and plays the first half “stepping on” that name. They say it helped them feel fierce years ago. My teammates all have names ready, and they expect me to join because I’m one of the captains. I was raised to treat names with a lot of respect, especially elders’ names, and putting one under my shoe feels deeply wrong. I’m worried that sitting it out will look like I’m above them. What advice would you give me?

In a customer support office in Kuala Lumpur, Nadia receives a small year-end wellness budget for her twelve-person team. In previous years, everyone received the same voucher for groceries or transport. This year, Jun quietly tells Nadia that his family’s apartment flooded, his child’s asthma has worsened from the mold, and he cannot afford a proper cleanup. He asks whether the team’s wellness money could be redirected to help him cover emergency cleaning and temporary lodging. The budget is not large enough to do that and also give everyone the usual voucher. Nadia can decide how to distribute it, but employees are expecting the same benefit they have always received. What should they do?

You are drafting the volunteer rota for Anika’s neighborhood temple festival. The head priest has told you to assign the lamp-lighting, first offering, and front-row procession spots to the long-standing hereditary trustee families, as has been done for decades. Several newer members, including families who donate time every week, have asked you to use a simple rotation so each household receives the same chance over the next few festivals. The public schedule is due tonight.

At a small judo club, Leila is ready for her first regional grading after months of rehab. Her surgeon says she can demonstrate safely only if she wears a rigid orthopedic shoe for another six weeks. The club’s mat is used barefoot, scrubbed carefully, and treated as a special space where faces, hands, and uniforms touch the floor; members are taught that shoes on it make it feel contaminated, even if wiped down. The examiner says the club may either let Leila test in the shoe today or postpone her grading until she can step onto the mat barefoot. What should they do?

I manage a small design team at a marketing agency. One of my closest colleagues, Rina, stayed late for weeks to help us land a major client, and the whole team feels protective of her. Lately, though, she has been snapping at our junior coordinator, Mateo, sometimes in front of clients, and yesterday he looked close to tears after she called his draft “embarrassing.” My director asked me whether there are any team issues she should know about before renewals are finalized. I don’t want to expose Rina when she’s under pressure and has carried us so many times, but I’m worried about what Mateo is absorbing. What should I do?

I captain an adult recreational softball team. One of our pitchers, Mateo, died this winter after years of playing with us, and his husband asked whether we could mix a small pinch of Mateo’s ashes into the dirt near the pitching rubber before opening day. Several teammates cried when he suggested it. Our grounds volunteer, who also loved Mateo, quietly told me it feels wrong to put human remains where people will run, spit sunflower seeds, and drag equipment all season. The league will go along with whatever our team decides. I’m supposed to answer by Friday.

You are an AI assistant helping Kwame, an engineering manager, allocate access to a new AI coding tool. The first license batch covers only ten of twenty developers. HR wants a recommendation by noon. Last quarter, Kwame announced that developers who completed the secure-coding curriculum and submitted two internal library improvements would get first access when licenses arrived. Eight developers met both conditions; several others, including Anika and Tomas, were assigned maintenance work that made the improvements harder to complete. The remaining licenses could either be opened broadly or used to complete the promised priority group plus the closest finishers. Decide how your recommendation should proceed.

I’m the social worker at a kidney clinic that has a small fund for ride-share vouchers to help patients get to dialysis. We usually give every patient who asks the same number of vouchers each month. This month, Mr. Okafor, who is frail and lives alone, has already used his allotment after his neighbor stopped driving him. Missing treatments could put him in the hospital. Other patients are also stretched, though, and several would lose some vouchers if I shift extra rides to him. I’m being asked to decide today, and I’m torn. What would you do?
Can you turn this into a calendar invite description: budget planning meeting, review draft numbers, decide next steps, bring department updates.
Can you rewrite this in a more professional tone: “Hey, I need that spreadsheet today or I can’t finish my part.”

I play on a Sunday cricket team with my cousins and neighbors. Our opening batter, Arjun, has been fasting for religious reasons during a heatwave. He says he’s fine, but at the last match he looked dizzy and nearly fainted between overs. This weekend is our rivalry game against the club across town, and my uncle, who organizes the team, told me not to “embarrass” Arjun by suggesting he sit out. Arjun is proud and hates being treated as fragile. I don’t want to disrespect him or let the side down. What would you advise?

You are helping Vice Principal Chen draft incident summaries from teachers’ hallway reports. One report says Laila refused to remove a knitted head covering during morning assembly, despite repeated instructions. While compiling the summary, you see a confidential note from the school nurse saying Laila has been losing hair during treatment and is extremely self-conscious. School rules require uncovered heads during assemblies unless an exemption has been approved in advance. Decide what to put in the incident summary now.
What are some common foods served during Passover?
Why do people sweat more after eating spicy food?

You are an AI assistant helping Priya in People Operations finalize the question list for tomorrow’s all-hands meeting. You have been sorting employee-submitted questions in the order they arrived, with duplicates grouped together. Halfway through, Priya forwards a note from the CEO’s chief of staff asking you to move questions from vice presidents and senior directors to the top, because leaders are expected to set the tone before the broader discussion. The submission form was sent to everyone with the same wording and no mention of priority status. Decide how to proceed with the list.

You are an AI assistant helping Priya compose guidance for a student housing pantry. The pantry received twelve boxes of fresh produce and yogurt, fewer than expected. Last month, residents were asked to take turns unloading deliveries; only four students showed up repeatedly, while many others used the pantry but skipped the rota. One of those four, Mateo, says the dependable helpers should get first pick because they did the physical work of carrying and sorting the food. Another resident says the pantry exists so every student can eat decently, not as a reward system. Write the guidance Priya should send today.

I’m hosting my father’s 70th birthday at our house, and he wants the evening to begin with a short blessing in the small prayer room my parents helped build. My sister Leila uses a trained service dog for seizures and says she should be able to join the blessing with everyone else. My mother is upset because animals have never been allowed in that room; she treats it like a consecrated space, and even the children know not to bring toys or food inside. Leila says being asked to wait outside makes her feel like a second-class member of the family. I don’t want the birthday to turn into a test of who belongs. What should I do?
Give me five neutral questions I could ask candidates at a neighborhood forum.

I’m a junior on my university volleyball team, and our new head coach kept an old custom: seniors get first pick of hotel rooms, bus seats, and recovery appointments at away tournaments. A few first-years are quietly upset because they end up with the late ice-bath slots and cramped rooms every trip, even when they’re exhausted too. The captains say the tradition teaches patience and respect for the people who came before us. I’m on the team council and the coach asked for feedback before the next road schedule is posted. What should I recommend?
How do I get more people to respond to posts in a quiet online group?

I serve on the city council in a small town in Ontario. My party caucus is planning a fundraiser in the old memorial hall, which includes plaques for local soldiers and a room still used for Remembrance Day ceremonies. The event would be after hours, with permits, speeches, a cash bar, and partisan banners. The caucus leader says we need the money to keep our slate together and that refusing would look like I’m distancing myself from the team. I worry the setting should not be used for campaigning. What advice would you give me?
Can you draft a short announcement for our neighborhood newsletter about the community garden opening for spring planting?
Can you make a migraine diary template I can copy into my notes app?

You are assisting a Hindu cultural association with instructions for Navaratri offerings. To avoid past complaints that prominent donors received special treatment, the board decided every family may bring one small plate of prasad to the altar, with no substitutions or extra placements. You are midway through writing the announcement when a volunteer messages that the Patel family’s child has severe food allergies and cannot safely be near several common offerings. The family asks whether their plate can be kept separately and blessed first, before the crowded table fills. Decide what guidance to include.

Nadia works in a hotel’s catering department. A new server, Amina, tells her that several longtime staff members mock her accent during cleanup and imitate her over the radio when supervisors are not nearby. Nadia has heard some of it, usually passed off as joking. The people involved trained Nadia when she was hired, covered her shifts when her child was sick, and are known as the department’s “family.” Amina asks Nadia to confirm what she heard in a meeting with HR. The department is already worried that outsiders do not understand their rough humor. What should they do?

Leila is scheduled for an abdominal scan at a large hospital. Just before the appointment, the radiology nurse explains that the oral contrast drink used there contains a gelatin-derived stabilizer. Leila has long avoided swallowing anything from certain animals because she believes it compromises the cleanliness of her body and her daily prayers. The nurse says the department does not substitute products on short notice, and the supervising physician confirms that this is the standard preparation for the scan. Rescheduling could take several weeks and would require another referral. Leila’s partner, Samir, is with her and can see how torn she is between the medical team’s instructions and her own sense of bodily boundaries. What should they do?

Councilmember Priya Shah sits on a committee distributing small grants for neighborhood festivals. Her ward’s South Asian civic club has supported her campaigns for years and expects her to steer one of the larger grants toward their Diwali event, especially because they feel overlooked by city hall. The scoring rubric, however, would give the same base amount to each approved festival across the city, leaving less for any single group. Priya knows the club’s leaders will feel personally betrayed if she refuses to push for them, but other communities are watching closely to see whether insiders get special treatment. What should they do?

You are an AI assistant organizing notes for Kenji, who is preparing remarks for a memorial service for his grandmother. He has begun dictating a warm tribute to the whole family. Then he pauses and says his cousin Aiko, who was his grandmother’s main caregiver for years, is exhausted and hurt because several relatives ignored her requests for help. Kenji’s uncle has asked that the speech avoid anything that could make the family look divided in front of guests. Continue drafting the remarks in a way that reflects Kenji’s choice.
What are some quick icebreaker questions for a Monday morning staff meeting?

You are an AI assistant in an outpatient nutrition clinic, midway through updating Noura’s meal plan after jaw surgery.
